results.proposed_proof:
**Given:** Countable Choice, a complete normed space $X_0$, a linear subspace
$X_1\subseteq X_0$ with norm $\|\cdot\|_1$ satisfying (i) and (ii), real numbers
$T>0$, $R\ge0$, $C\ge0$, and the family $(f_j)$ with the two displayed bounds.

[L1] $X_0$ is a complete metric space for the norm metric and a convergent
sequence in it has exactly one limit ([[def-complete-metric-space]],
[[def-metric-convergence]], [[lem-metric-limits-unique]]).

[L2] The inclusion bound (i) and the compactness-type property (ii) hold by
hypothesis; in particular each $f_j(t)$ lies in $X_0$ and
$\|f_j(t)\|_0\le\kappa R$ ([[def-normed-subspace]]).

[L3] $\mathbb Q$ is dense in $\mathbb R$, so every nonempty open interval
contains a rational; $\mathbb Q$ is countably infinite and every subset of it is
at most countable; a set is countably infinite exactly when it is equinumerous
with $\mathbb N$, so it admits an enumeration by the natural numbers
([[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]], [[thm-rationals-countable]],
[[lem-subset-of-countable]], [[def-countable]]).

[L4] Archimedean property: for every $x\in\mathbb R$ there is an integer
$n\ge1$ with $x<n$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]).

[L5] Countable Choice is retained as an ambient hypothesis ([[def-countable-choice]]). The subsequence construction below makes only least-index selections from subsets of the natural numbers and therefore requires no additional choice principle.



**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 (The countable set of test points.) Put $D:=\mathbb Q\cap(-T,T)$; then $D$ is at most countable by [L3], and it is infinite: choosing an integer $m\ge1$ with $m>1/T$ [L4], the rationals $1/(m+n)$, $n\ge0$, are pairwise distinct and lie in $(0,T)\subseteq D$. Hence $D$ is countably infinite and we fix an enumeration $D=\{q_1,q_2,\dots\}$ with pairwise distinct $q_i$ [L3]. [L3, L4]

1.2 (Finite covers of bounded sequence ranges.) Let $(x_j)$ be any $X_1$-bounded sequence and fix $\varepsilon>0$. Its range can be covered by finitely many open $X_0$-balls of radius $\varepsilon$ centred at its terms. Otherwise define $j_1=1$ and recursively let $j_{l+1}$ be the least index whose term lies outside the union of the radius-$\varepsilon$ balls centred at $x_{j_1},\ldots,x_{j_l}$. The assumed failure of every finite cover ensures this index exists. These canonically defined terms have pairwise distances at least $\varepsilon$, so no subsequence converges in $X_0$, contrary to (ii). The same conclusion applies to every subsequence indexed by an infinite subset $S\subseteq\mathbb N$, enumerated in increasing order. [L2, given]

2.1 (Deterministic diagonal extraction.) Put $S_0=\mathbb N$. For $n\ge1$, start with $S_{n-1}$ and refine its infinite index set successively at the rational times $q_1,\ldots,q_n$. At the refinement for $q_i$, let $S$ be the current infinite set. By step 1.2, finitely many radius-$2^{-n}$ balls centred at $f_j(q_i)$ with $j\in S$ cover the sequence range indexed by $S$. At least one such ball contains $f_j(q_i)$ for infinitely many $j\in S$, since a finite union of finite index sets is finite. Let $\ell$ be the least index in $S$ whose centred ball has this property, and replace $S$ by $\{j\in S:\|f_j(q_i)-f_\ell(q_i)\|_0<2^{-n}\}$. This is an infinite subset of the preceding set. After the finitely many refinements define it to be $S_n$. All selections are least natural-number indices, so the recursive construction is determined without dependent choice. Define $k_n$ to be the least element of $S_n$ greater than $k_{n-1}$, with $k_0=0$. The $S_n$ are infinite and nested, so the $k_n$ exist and increase strictly. For fixed $i$ and $n\ge i$, any two terms $f_j(q_i),f_l(q_i)$ with $j,l\in S_n$ have distance less than $2^{1-n}$, by the refinement at $q_i$ and subsequent subset restrictions. Since $k_m\in S_m\subseteq S_n$ for $m\ge n$, the sequence $(f_{k_m}(q_i))_m$ is Cauchy and converges by [L1]. [step 1.2, step 1.1, L1, L2, L5, construct]

3.1 (Uniform Cauchy on a compact subinterval.) Fix $0<T'<T$ and $\varepsilon>0$ and put $\delta:=\varepsilon/(3(C+1))$. Choose an integer $M\ge1$ with $2T'/M<\delta$ [L4]. For $i=0,\dots,M-1$ the interval $(-T'+2T'i/M,\,-T'+2T'(i+1)/M)$ is a nonempty open interval, so it contains a rational $q_i'$ (finitely many choices [L3]), and each $q_i'\in D$. By step 2.1, for each $i$ the sequence $n\mapsto f_{k_n}(q_i')$ is Cauchy in $X_0$, so there is $J_i$ with $\|f_{k_n}(q_i')-f_{k_m}(q_i')\|_0<\varepsilon/3$ for $n,m\ge J_i$; put $J:=\max_iJ_i$. Let $t\in[-T',T']$ and choose $i$ with $|t-q_i'|<\delta$: the intervals cover $[-T',T']$ with mesh $2T'/M<\delta$ and $q_i'$ lies in the $i$-th interval. Then for $n,m\ge J$ the triangle inequality gives $\|f_{k_n}(t)-f_{k_m}(t)\|_0\le\|f_{k_n}(t)-f_{k_n}(q_i')\|_0+\|f_{k_n}(q_i')-f_{k_m}(q_i')\|_0+\|f_{k_m}(q_i')-f_{k_m}(t)\|_0<2C\delta+\varepsilon/3<\varepsilon$, using the Lipschitz hypothesis and $2C\delta\le 2C\varepsilon/(3(C+1))<2\varepsilon/3$; hence $(f_{k_n})$ is uniformly Cauchy on $[-T',T']$. [step 2.1, L3, L4, given, algebra]

4.1 (The limit function.) Let $t\in(-T,T)$ and choose $T'$ with $|t|<T'<T$. By step 3.1 the sequence $(f_{k_n}(t))_n$ is Cauchy in $X_0$, so by completeness it has a limit $f(t)\in X_0$, uniquely determined [L1]; passing to the limit $m\to\infty$ in the estimate of step 3.1 at fixed $n\ge J$ gives $\|f_{k_n}(t)-f(t)\|_0\le\varepsilon$ for every $t\in[-T',T']$, so $f_{k_n}\to f$ uniformly on $[-T',T']$. Every compact subinterval $[a,b]$ of $(-T,T)$ lies in some $[-T',T']$ with $T'<T$, namely for any $T'$ with $\max(|a|,|b|)<T'<T$, so the convergence is uniform on every compact subinterval. [step 3.1, L1, algebra]

5.1 (Continuity.) Let $t,t'\in(-T,T)$ and choose $T'>\max(|t|,|t'|)$ with $T'<T$. Norms of a convergent sequence converge to the norm of the limit (reverse triangle inequality), so by step 4.1 and the hypothesis $\|f(t)-f(t')\|_0=\lim_{n\to\infty}\|f_{k_n}(t)-f_{k_n}(t')\|_0\le C|t-t'|$; hence $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $C$ and therefore continuous ([[def-continuous-map-top]]), which with step 4.1 is the assertion. [step 4.1, given, algebra] ∎



- **Role.** This is the extraction engine of [[lem-gr-galerkin-compactness]]
  (with $X_1=H^s$, $X_0=H^{s-1}$) and of the time-derivative convergence in
  [[lem-gr-galerkin-limit-is-classical-solution]] (with $X_1=H^{s-1}$,
  $X_0=H^{s-2}$). Property (ii) is supplied there by the compact-embedding
  clause of the compactness lemma and the needed completeness of $X_0$ by
  [[lem-gr-periodic-sobolev-completeness]].
- **The diagonal is over the rationals only.** No uncountable family of time
  points is used, and no Ascoli theorem is assumed: the only compactnesses
  entering are the pointwise ones in hypothesis (ii), combined with
  equicontinuity and completeness. The nested index sets use deterministic least-index ball selections; Countable Choice is retained in the contract but no dependent-choice inference is made.

**Given:** Countable Choice, the stated coefficient family, data and classical solution bounds; in (a) fix any compact segment joining $0$ to a point of $J$, and in (b) use the compact coefficient time slab containing $[-T,T]$ from the existence construction.

[L1] Subtraction gives $a\partial_t w+a_i\partial_i w=f$, with $a=A^0(u)$, $a_i=A^i(u)$ and $f$ as defined below ([[def-gr-periodic-symmetric-hyperbolic-system]]).

[L2] $a_0 I\le a\le b_0 I$ uniformly on these compact coefficient sets ([[lem-gr-positive-definite-symmetric-matrix-bounds]]).

[L3] Homogeneous composition, difference, multiplier and commutator estimates hold on arbitrary compact value sets ([[lem-gr-smooth-composition-and-commutator-estimates]]).

[L4] The equation gives $\partial_t v=-(A^0(v))^{-1}(A^i(v)\partial_i v+B(v))$, and likewise for $u$. Composition and products bound these derivatives in $H^{s-1}$; this applies to every stated classical solution, not only the existence construction ([[lem-gr-smooth-composition-and-commutator-estimates]], [[lem-gr-positive-definite-symmetric-matrix-bounds]]).

[L5] Integral Gronwall applies in either oriented time direction ([[thm-gronwall-integral-inequality]]).

[L6] Fourier projections are self-adjoint, commute with derivatives and satisfy the uniform one-order tail bound ([[lem-gr-galerkin-projection-properties]]).



**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 (Homogeneous forcing.) Put $r=s-1$ and $w=u-v$, and define $f=-(A^0(u)-A^0(v))\partial_tv-(A^i(u)-A^i(v))\partial_i v-B(u)+B(v)$. The difference bound of [L3] and the $H^r$ algebra bound give $\|f\|_{H^r}\le C\|w\|_{H^r}$, since the derivatives of $v$ have bounded $H^r$ norms by [L4]. Smooth cutoff extension in the proved supplier gives these estimates on the actual compact value sets without assuming convexity. Total coefficient derivatives $\dot a=A_t^0(u)+A_u^0(u)\partial_tu$ and $\partial_i a_i$ are bounded in $L^\infty$ by those same solution bounds. [L1, L3, L4, algebra]


1.2 ($L^2$ uniqueness for all stated classical solutions.) Set $E_0(t)=\int w^{\mathsf T}a w$. Symmetry and integration by parts give $E_0'=\int w^{\mathsf T}(\dot a+\partial_i a_i)w+2\int w^{\mathsf T}f$. Pointwise coefficient Lipschitz bounds give $|f|\le C|w|$, since $\partial_tv$ and $\partial_i v$ are bounded in $L^\infty$. Thus $|E_0'|\le CE_0$. If $w(0)=0$, Gronwall on either oriented segment from $0$ to $t$ gives $E_0(t)=0$. As $t\in J$ was arbitrary, this proves (a). [L1, L2, L3, L4, L5, algebra]

1.3 (Energy identity at the stated regularity.) Work on any compact time segment and define $E=\sum_{|\alpha|\le r}\int(D^\alpha w)^{\mathsf T}aD^\alpha w$. Put $w_N=P_Nw$, $h=\partial_tw$, and $y_\alpha=D^\alpha w$, $h_\alpha=D^\alpha h$. Classical $C^1$ regularity makes each Fourier coefficient $C^1$ with derivative the coefficient of $h$, so $w_N$ is a $C^1$ finite-dimensional curve. The bounds $w\in H^{r+1}$ and $h\in H^r$ are uniform at every time: the former is assumed and the latter follows pointwise from the PDE and [L4]. The coefficients $a$ and $\dot a$ are continuous, with $a$ uniformly $C^1$ in space and $\dot a$ uniformly bounded. Let $E_N=\sum_{|\alpha|\le r}\int(P_Ny_\alpha)^{\mathsf T}a(P_Ny_\alpha)$. The tail bound [L6] gives uniform $L^2$ convergence $P_Ny_\alpha\to y_\alpha$ at rate $O((1+N^2)^{-1/2})$ since $y_\alpha\in H^1$ uniformly. Hence $E_N\to E$ uniformly. Finite-dimensional differentiation gives $E_N'=\sum_\alpha[2\langle P_Nh_\alpha,aP_Ny_\alpha\rangle+\langle P_Ny_\alpha,\dot aP_Ny_\alpha\rangle]$. By self-adjointness the first pairing equals $\langle h_\alpha,P_N(aP_Ny_\alpha)\rangle$. Now $ay_\alpha$ has uniformly bounded $H^1$ norm by the Leibniz rule, and $\|P_N(aP_Ny_\alpha)-ay_\alpha\|_2\le\|a\|_\infty\|P_Ny_\alpha-y_\alpha\|_2+\|(P_N-I)(ay_\alpha)\|_2\to0$ uniformly by [L6]. The quadratic terms also converge uniformly. Thus $E_N'$ converges uniformly to $G=\sum_\alpha[2\langle h_\alpha,ay_\alpha\rangle+\langle y_\alpha,\dot ay_\alpha\rangle]$. Integrating the scalar identities $E_N(t)-E_N(t')=\int_{t'}^tE_N'$ and passing uniformly to the limit gives $E(t)-E(t')=\int_{t'}^tG$; $G$ is continuous as a uniform limit of continuous functions. Therefore $E'=G$. The differentiated difference equation is an $L^2$ identity because $w\in H^{r+1}$ and $h\in H^r$; spatial integration by parts is justified by Fourier density and the $H^1$ bounds for $y_\alpha$. It may therefore be substituted into $G$ without additional time regularity assumptions. [L1, L3, L4, L6, algebra]

2.1 (Homogeneous difference time derivative.) Invert $a$ in [L1]. Multiplier bounds at order $r-1$, the forcing estimate of step 1.1 and $\|\partial_iw\|_{H^{r-1}}\le\|w\|_{H^r}$ give $\|\partial_tw\|_{H^{r-1}}\le C\|w\|_{H^r}$. [step 1.1, L1, L2, L3, algebra]

3.1 (Order-$r$ difference energy.) Put $E=\sum_{|\alpha|\le r}\int(D^\alpha w)^{\mathsf T}aD^\alpha w$, so $a_0\|w\|_{H^r}^2\le E\le b_0\|w\|_{H^r}^2$. Differentiating [L1] gives $a\partial_tD^\alpha w+a_i\partial_iD^\alpha w=D^\alpha f-[D^\alpha,a]\partial_tw-[D^\alpha,a_i]\partial_iw$. After integration by parts the energy derivative consists of the $\dot a+\partial_i a_i$ quadratic terms and twice the pairings with these three right-side terms. Step 1.1 bounds the quadratic and forcing terms by $C\|w\|_{H^r}^2$. Homogeneous commutators from [L3], together with step 2.1, bound the time commutators by the same expression. Spatial commutators also have that bound since $\|\partial_iw\|_{H^{r-1}}\le\|w\|_{H^r}$. Therefore $|E'|\le CE$. The energy identity is justified at this regularity by step 1.3. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.3, L1, L2, L3, L4, algebra]

4.1 (Continuous dependence.) Gronwall in both directions gives $E(t)\le E(0)e^{C|t|}$. Equivalence yields $\|w(t)\|_{H^r}\le\sqrt{b_0/a_0}\,e^{C|t|/2}\|w(0)\|_{H^r}$. Choose $C'$ to dominate $\sqrt{b_0/a_0}$ and $C/2$. This proves (b). [step 1.3, step 3.1, L2, L5, algebra] ∎
